titleDv: ޤާނޫނު ނަންބަރު 12/2016 (ޖިނާއީ އިޖުރާއަތުގެ ޤާނޫނު) އަށް ... ވަނަ އިސްލާހު ގެނައުމުގެ ބިލު
summary: This bill amends the Criminal Procedure Act (Law No. 12/2016), mainly its rules on sharing evidence before a criminal trial. It rewrites the list of material the prosecution does not have to hand to the accused, such as internal investigation documents, the identity of people in secret operations and some witness statements, and sets out when a court can order evidence withheld, delayed or shared only under conditions. It gives the defence a matching but shorter set of protections, limits how the accused may use disclosed material, and repeals sections 192 to 197 and 202, which cover court orders to confiscate money and property gained through crime and appeals against those orders.
whyItMatters: It changes what evidence an accused person and their lawyer can see before trial and what they may do with it. It also removes the Act's confiscation rules, which the government links to a separate bill on property obtained through crime.
keyProvisions: Section 130 replaced: the State need not disclose its internal investigation and prosecution documents (opinions, legal advice, analyses, communications between investigators and prosecutors), information identifying people who ran a secret operation, certain State witness statements, or anything another law exempts; redacted parts must still be shared, and withheld evidence must be shared as soon as the reason ends, even mid-trial.

Section 131(n) replaced: the court may withhold, delay or condition disclosure of State evidence if it would be unfair because of risk of harm or threats, revealing investigation operations, tampering with evidence, exposing a third party's personal data, privileged material, enabling further crime, contempt of court, or exposing a trade secret; new 131(r) defines 'trade secret' and the State must give its reasons when it asks for protection.

New section 131-1: the accused may use evidence disclosed by the State only to prepare their defence or for their lawyer's official duties, and may not share it with anyone other than people working under them.

Sections 133 and 134 amended for the defence: work prepared by the accused, their lawyer or the lawyer's staff need not be disclosed, and the defence may seek a protective order only on grounds of harm or threats and evidence tampering, stating its reasons.

Sections 192 to 197 (court orders to confiscate money and property gained through crime, later-found assets, substitute assets, third-party rights and enforcement) and section 202 (appeals against confiscation orders) are repealed.
Section 13 of the bill: the changes take effect 6 months after the law is ratified and published in the Government Gazette.
whoIsAffected: People accused of crimes and their lawyers, prosecutors, police and other investigators, witnesses, and businesses whose information appears in evidence.
statedReasons: The government says it wants to review the rules on disclosing evidence in criminal cases and make the changes to this Act needed in connection with the bill on property obtained through crime.
